questions.q: A base class must provide a default shipping calculation that works on its own. Subclasses may optionally replace it. Code must be able to create the base class directly. How should it be declared?
options: public abstract class Shipper { public abstract Decimal calc(); }
public interface Shipper { Decimal calc(); }
public class Shipper { public Decimal calc() {...} }
public virtual class Shipper { public virtual Decimal calc() {...} }
questions.explain: A virtual class can be instantiated and extended. A virtual method has a default body that subclasses can override with the override keyword.
wrong: Abstract classes can't be instantiated, and abstract methods have no default body.
Interfaces have no implementation and can't be instantiated.
Non-virtual classes are final, so they can't be extended.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Extending a Class / Virtual and Abstract

questions.q: An org has three triggers on Opportunity written by different teams, and their order of execution is unpredictable. What best practice addresses this?
options: Add a static Boolean to each trigger
One trigger per object that delegates to a handler class
Move all the logic into a single @future method called from each trigger
Use the Trigger Order field to number the triggers
questions.explain: With one trigger per object and a handler class, you control the order, testing gets simpler, and recursion handling lives in one place.
wrong: A static flag helps with recursion, not ordering across triggers.
Async logic changes the behaviour (no before-save changes) and doesn't fix the design.
Apex triggers have no such field. Their order isn't guaranteed.
questions.source: Trailhead: Apex Triggers best practices; Apex Developer Guide: Triggers

questions.q: What happens when the developer saves Child?
options: It compiles; Child replaces run()
Compile error: Parent is not virtual or abstract, so it can't be extended
It compiles, but Parent.run() always executes at runtime
Compile error only because Child is missing the override keyword
questions.explain: Apex classes are final by default. Parent must be virtual or abstract to be extended, and run() must be virtual with override in Child to be replaced.
wrong: Apex doesn't allow extending a final class.
The class never compiles, so nothing runs.
override is also needed, but the first error is that Parent can't be extended.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Extending a Class

questions.q: A team adopts the Apex Enterprise Patterns (service, domain, selector, unit of work). Which two responsibilities are assigned correctly? (Choose 2)
options: Selector layer: encapsulates SOQL queries for an object
Domain layer: owns all HTTP callouts for the org
Service layer: exposes business operations and defines the transaction boundary
Selector layer: performs all DML for the object
Unit of Work: executes each DML statement as soon as it is registered
questions.explain: Selectors centralize queries. Services expose business operations and own the transaction.
wrong: Domain classes hold object-specific behaviour and validation, not org-wide callouts.
DML is coordinated by the unit of work, not selectors.
The unit of work collects DML and commits it together later.
questions.source: Trailhead: Apex Enterprise Patterns (Service Layer, Domain & Selector Layers)

questions.q: Which declaration creates a valid custom exception?
options: public class InventoryError extends Exception {}
public class InventoryException implements Exception {}
public class InventoryException extends Exception {}
public exception InventoryException {}
questions.explain: Custom exceptions extend Exception, and the class name must end with "Exception".
wrong: The name must end in "Exception".
Exception is a class to extend, not an interface.
Apex has no "exception" keyword for declarations.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Create Custom Exceptions

questions.q: Review the code below. Which two statements are true after it runs? (Choose 2)
options: The setSavepoint and rollback calls don't count toward DML limits
The Contact remains in the database
c.Id still contains a value after the rollback
The Account remains in the database
The static counter is reset to 0
questions.explain: Rollback undoes only DML after the savepoint, so the Account stays. IDs aren't cleared from rolled-back sObjects, so c.Id keeps its value.
wrong: Both setSavepoint and rollback count toward the DML statement limit.
The Contact insert happened after the savepoint, so it is rolled back.
Static variables aren't reverted by a rollback.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control

questions.q: A batch method sometimes hits "Too many SOQL queries: 101". A developer wraps the logic in try/catch(Exception e) to log the error and continue. What happens?
options: The catch block logs the error and processing continues
The LimitException can't be caught, and the transaction stops
Only the last query is rolled back
The platform retries the transaction automatically
questions.explain: System.LimitException can't be caught. Prevent it with bulkified design and checks such as Limits.getQueries().
wrong: Limit exceptions skip all catch blocks.
The whole transaction is rolled back.
There is no automatic retry.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Exception Statements / Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: When importing 200 leads, one bad record must not stop the valid ones from saving. The developer also needs to know which records failed and why. What should be used?
options: insert leads; inside try/catch
insert as user leads;
Database.setSavepoint() before insert leads; then roll back only the failed rows
Database.insert(leads, false) and check each SaveResult
questions.explain: With allOrNone=false, the valid records save. Each SaveResult reports isSuccess() and getErrors() for its record.
wrong: A plain insert is all-or-nothing. One failure rolls back the whole batch.
User mode enforces permissions but is still all-or-nothing.
A savepoint rolls back everything after it. It can't keep the valid rows or report per-record errors.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Database Class Methods / SaveResult

questions.q: Which two statements about Platform Cache are true? (Choose 2)
options: Cached values can be evicted before their TTL expires, so code must handle a cache miss
Org cache values are guaranteed to persist for 48 hours
Org cache is visible only to the user who stored the value
Values stored in Platform Cache count against data storage
Session cache is tied to an individual user's session
questions.explain: The cache is best-effort, so always handle null. Session cache is per user session, while org cache is shared across users.
wrong: 48 hours is the maximum TTL, not a guarantee.
Org cache is shared by all users.
Cache uses partition capacity, not data storage.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Platform Cache

questions.q: Currency conversion rates are read thousands of times a day by all users and change once a day. A developer wants a single call that returns the cached rate, or loads it with SOQL and caches it on a miss. What should they build?
options: A Cache.CacheBuilder class with doLoad(), read via Cache.Org.get(RateLoader.class, key)
A Session cache entry populated by each user's first query
A static Map in a singleton class populated on first use
A hierarchy custom setting kept current by a trigger on CurrencyType, read with getOrgDefaults()
questions.explain: CacheBuilder runs doLoad() automatically on a cache miss and stores the result in org cache, which is shared across users and transactions.
wrong: Session cache isn't shared, so every user would reload the data.
Statics last only one transaction.
CurrencyType doesn't support Apex triggers, and a setting synced by extra automation is more fragile than a cache that loads itself.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: CacheBuilder Interface

questions.q: A singleton class caches a configuration map in a private static variable. Does the cached map carry over to the next, separate request from the same user?
options: Yes, a private static in a singleton persists for the rest of the user's session
Yes, for up to 24 hours
No, statics last one transaction. Use Platform Cache to share across requests
No, unless the class is declared with sharing
questions.explain: Apex statics are scoped to a single transaction. Platform Cache (org or session) keeps data across requests.
wrong: That describes session cache, not statics.
That is the org cache default TTL, not static behaviour.
Sharing keywords don't affect how long a static lives.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Static and Instance Methods, Variables / Platform Cache

questions.q: A developer is writing a utility class that is called from many places. It should run in the caller's sharing mode, and with sharing when it is the entry point of a transaction. Which declaration fits?
options: public without sharing class RecordUtil
public inherited sharing class RecordUtil
public class RecordUtil (no sharing keyword at all)
public with sharing class RecordUtil
questions.explain: inherited sharing runs in the calling class's sharing mode, and with sharing when the class is the entry point (for example an LWC controller). It also makes the intent explicit.
wrong: This always ignores sharing rules, whoever calls it.
In classic behaviour a class with no keyword runs without sharing when it is the entry point, so it isn't safe there.
This always enforces sharing, even when called from a without sharing class.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using the with sharing, without sharing, and inherited sharing Keywords

questions.q: A multi-currency org stores opportunities in several currencies. Which field tells Apex which currency an Opportunity's Amount is in?
options: DefaultCurrencyIsoCode on the Opportunity record
CurrencyType, a lookup on each record to the currency
CurrencyIsoCode on the Opportunity record
UserInfo.getDefaultCurrency() for the record owner
questions.explain: When multi-currency is enabled, every record with currency fields gets a CurrencyIsoCode field naming that record's currency.
wrong: DefaultCurrencyIsoCode is the personal currency on the User record, not a record's currency.
CurrencyType is the object that lists the org's currencies and rates; records don't look it up.
That returns the running user's currency, which can differ from the record's currency.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Manage Multiple Currencies; Object Reference: CurrencyType

questions.q: A logging utility receives record Ids from many objects (Accounts, Cases, custom objects) and must branch on the object type. It is called in loops, so it must be cheap. What should the developer use?
options: recordId.getSObjectType(), then compare it with tokens like Account.SObjectType
Query each candidate object with WHERE Id = :recordId until one of the queries returns a row
Loop over Schema.getGlobalDescribe() and compare each object's getKeyPrefix() with the Id's prefix
Compare String.valueOf(recordId).left(3) with key prefixes hard-coded for each object
questions.explain: Id.getSObjectType() returns the token for the Id's object without a query or a global describe. Comparing tokens is fast and safe.
wrong: This wastes SOQL queries and fails on objects you didn't list.
It works, but a global describe is expensive, especially inside a loop.
Custom object key prefixes differ between orgs, so hard-coded prefixes break.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Id Class (getSObjectType)

questions.q: A developer adds a payment provider that implements an existing interface. What happens when CardPay is saved?
options: It compiles, because interface methods take the class's default access
It compiles, and charge() stays private to CardPay as declared
Compile error: CardPay must also be declared virtual to implement an interface
Compile error: the implementation of charge() must be public or global
questions.explain: Interface methods have the interface's access level, so the implementing class must declare them public or global. With no modifier an Apex method is private, so CardPay doesn't compile.
wrong: The default (private) access doesn't match the interface, so it is rejected.
An interface method can't be implemented as private; the class doesn't compile.
Implementing an interface doesn't need virtual; virtual is about being extended.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Interfaces; Access Modifiers

questions.q: A service catches a DmlException and must throw its own OrderException, keeping the original error as the cause for logging. Which line does this?
options: throw (OrderException) e;
throw new OrderException(e.getMessage() + e.getCause());
throw new OrderException('Order save failed', e);
throw new OrderException('Order save failed').setCause(e);
questions.explain: Custom exceptions get a (String message, Exception cause) constructor for free. The caller can then read the original error with getCause().
wrong: A DmlException is never an OrderException, so this cast fails.
This only copies text into the message; no cause is kept.
Exceptions have no setCause() method. Use the (message, cause) constructor or initCause().
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Create Custom Exceptions; Exception Class and Built-In Exceptions

questions.q: In Cache.Org.getPartition('local.Rates'), what does the prefix 'local' mean?
options: The partition is stored only on the local app server
The org's own namespace, used for partitions you created
The partition is visible only to the current user's session
A partition that is cleared when the transaction ends
questions.explain: 'local' stands for the org's default namespace, so you can name a partition without hard-coding a namespace. In an installed managed package it refers to the subscriber org's namespace.
wrong: Platform Cache is a shared service; 'local' is about namespaces, not servers.
Per-user visibility is what session cache gives you, not the 'local' prefix.
Cached values outlive the transaction until their TTL ends or they are evicted.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Org Class (Cache Key Format)

questions.q: A multi-page wizard must remember one user's in-progress choices for an hour or two, and other users must never see them. Where should the developer cache the data?
options: A hierarchy custom setting record for each user, written by DML on every wizard step
Org cache with the user's Id in each key, so the values can live for up to 48 hours
A static variable in the wizard's Apex controller, which lasts for the whole user session
Session cache, which is tied to that user's session and holds values for up to 8 hours
questions.explain: Session cache stores data for one user's session, for up to 8 hours. Org cache is shared by every user, and statics don't survive between requests.
wrong: That adds DML on every step and stores temporary data permanently.
Org cache is shared by all users, so any code could read these values; session cache is built for per-user data.
Statics last only one transaction, not a whole session.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Platform Cache

questions.q: Recruiting runs on the custom object Job__c, whose organization-wide default is Public Read Only. A trigger (saved at API version 62.0) shares each new job with the recruiter in the Recruiter__c lookup. The recruiting director says the code was copied from an older org where Job__c was Private. What happens when a job is inserted?
options: The share is created and the recruiter keeps Read access even after an owner change
Each share fails with FIELD_FILTER_VALIDATION_EXCEPTION, but the jobs still save
The whole transaction rolls back with a DmlException, so the job is not saved
The share is inserted and silently upgraded to Edit so it grants more than the OWD
questions.explain: A share row must grant access higher than the object's org-wide default. Read on a Public Read Only object is a trivial share, so each insert fails with FIELD_FILTER_VALIDATION_EXCEPTION. With allOrNone = false the jobs still save.
wrong: A share must grant more than the OWD. Read on a Public Read Only object is rejected.
allOrNone is false, so failures are returned in the SaveResults instead of thrown.
Salesforce never upgrades the requested access level on its own.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Sharing a Record Using Apex

questions.q: When the Recruiter__c lookup on a Job__c changes, a developer wants the new recruiter to get the old recruiter's Apex managed share. Job__c is Private, the Recruiter__c sharing reason exists, and the code is saved at API version 62.0. A tester reports an error when the lookup is changed. What is wrong?
options: RowCause must be set again on every update, or it resets to Manual
Share records can only be changed by a user with Modify All Data, even from Apex
UserOrGroupId can't be updated on a share. Delete the old share and insert a new one
update isn't supported on share objects; only insert and delete are, even for AccessLevel
questions.explain: ParentId, UserOrGroupId and RowCause can't be updated after a share is created. To move access to another user, delete the old share and insert a new one. (The code also has a query inside a loop, which a bulk fix should remove.)
wrong: RowCause can't be changed after creation, and it is not reset by an update.
Apex runs the DML. The Modify All Data rule applies to editing Apex managed shares in the UI.
AccessLevel on a share can be updated. Only ParentId, UserOrGroupId and RowCause are fixed.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Sharing a Record Using Apex

questions.q: A recruiting app grants access to Job__c records with Apex sharing reasons. Sometimes record locking stops shares from being written, so the architect wants an Apex managed sharing recalculation class. Which two statements about that class are true? (Choose 2)
options: It must implement Schedulable, and Salesforce runs it nightly
It implements Database.Batchable and is added on Job__c's Apex Sharing Recalculation list
It runs automatically every time a Job__c record changes owner
It runs automatically when the organization-wide default of Job__c changes, and an admin can also start it
It can only be started from Setup or by an OWD change, never from Apex with Database.executeBatch
questions.explain: A sharing recalculation class is a Database.Batchable class registered on the object's Apex Sharing Recalculation related list. It runs when the object's OWD changes, can be started by an admin, and can also be run with Database.executeBatch.
wrong: It implements Database.Batchable. Salesforce doesn't schedule it nightly.
An owner change doesn't start a recalculation. Apex managed shares simply survive it.
The docs say Database.executeBatch can start the recalculation programmatically.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Recalculating Apex Managed Sharing

questions.q: This execute method belongs to the sharing recalculation class for Job__c (API version 62.0). Record owners also share jobs by hand with the Sharing button, and another app uses a Hiring_Manager__c sharing reason on the same object. What is the main problem with the code?
options: New shares must be inserted in finish(), not in execute()
A recalculation class can't run DML itself. It must return the new share rows to the platform in finish()
AccessLevel 'Edit' isn't allowed during a recalculation, only 'Read'
The delete has no RowCause filter, so it removes every share on the jobs, not just Recruiter__c ones
questions.explain: A recalculation should delete and rebuild only the shares it manages, filtered by its own Apex sharing reason. Without a RowCause filter the query also picks up manual shares, other reasons' shares and owner rows.
wrong: execute() runs once per chunk and is where the shares for that chunk are rebuilt.
The class does its own delete and insert, like any batch class.
Read and Edit are both valid in a recalculation.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Recalculating Apex Managed Sharing

questions.q: Account OWD is Private. Each account has a Customer_Success_Manager__c user lookup, and that user needs Edit access. A developer writes the code below in a helper class and tries to save it. What happens?
options: It doesn't compile: AccountShare uses AccountId and AccountAccessLevel, not ParentId and AccessLevel
It inserts a Manual share that gives the manager Edit access
It compiles, but fails at runtime because standard objects like Account can't be shared from Apex code
It compiles, but the share is removed by the next sharing recalculation
questions.explain: Standard share objects name their fields after the object: AccountShare has AccountId and AccountAccessLevel, along with OpportunityAccessLevel and CaseAccessLevel. ParentId and AccessLevel are the field names on custom __Share objects.
wrong: The field names are wrong for AccountShare, so the class doesn't save.
Apex can insert AccountShare rows. The problem here is the field names.
The code never gets that far. It doesn't compile.
questions.source: Object Reference for the Salesforce Platform: AccountShare

questions.q: Invoice_Line__c is the detail in a master-detail relationship with Invoice__c, which is Private. A developer wants an auditor to see one line, and writes the code below. It doesn't compile. Why?
options: Invoice_Line__c's OWD must first be changed to Private
An Apex sharing reason must be created on Invoice_Line__c first
The class must be declared without sharing to reference share objects like Invoice_Line__Share
Detail objects have no share object. Share the master Invoice__c record instead
questions.explain: Detail records in a master-detail relationship have no share object. Their access follows the master record and the relationship's sharing setting, so Apex shares the parent Invoice__c.
wrong: A detail object's access is Controlled by Parent. Its OWD can't be set on its own.
A sharing reason can't create a share object that doesn't exist.
Sharing keywords don't decide whether a type exists.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Sharing a Record Using Apex

questions.q: A grants app shares each Grant__c (OWD Private) with reviewers through Apex managed sharing. The team is writing the sharing service. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: UserOrGroupId can hold a public group or a role group, not just a single user
UserOrGroupId can be the site guest user, so anonymous visitors can read approved grants
AccessLevel 'All' can be granted if the running user has Modify All Data
The grant's owner can remove an Apex managed share with the Sharing button
If a user has a Manual Read share and Apex inserts a Manual Edit share for the same user and record, the existing row is updated to Edit
questions.explain: Shares can target users, public groups or role groups. Inserting a higher-access manual share for the same user updates the existing row to the higher level instead of adding a duplicate.
wrong: Apex can't grant record access to unauthenticated guest users.
All is an internal value that can't be granted through a share row.
Only users with Modify All Data can add or change Apex managed sharing on a record.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Sharing a Record Using Apex

questions.q: Each Grant__c (OWD Private) must be editable by the reviewers listed in its child Grant_Reviewer__c junction records. Reviewers come from many roles and change weekly. Access must survive when a grant moves to a new owner and must go away when a reviewer row is deleted. Which two parts should the solution include? (Choose 2)
options: A criteria-based sharing rule on Grant__c that matches the reviewer users listed in the junction rows
A flow that sends the owner a reminder to click Sharing for each new reviewer
An Apex sharing reason on Grant__c, used as the RowCause of every Grant__Share the code writes
A Grant_Reviewer__c trigger that inserts a Grant__Share on insert and deletes the matching share on delete
Make Grant__c the detail side of a master-detail relationship with Grant_Reviewer__c
questions.explain: The rule depends on child records, so declarative sharing can't express it. Apex managed sharing with its own sharing reason survives owner changes, and a junction trigger adds and removes shares as reviewers change.
wrong: Sharing rules match record field values to groups or roles. They can't read users from child junction records.
Manual shares aren't automatic, and the Manual row cause is deleted when the owner changes.
That would remove Grant__c's own share object, and access would come from a single master record.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Sharing a Record Using Apex

questions.q: A support LWC calls CaseController.countAll(). The running agent can see 40 of the org's 500 cases. What does the method return?
options: 40, because the entry-point class is with sharing
40, because inherited sharing passes the with sharing mode down to every class it calls, CaseRepo included
500, because the query is in a without sharing class, and SYSTEM_MODE leaves sharing to it
A QueryException, because COUNT() can't be combined with WITH SYSTEM_MODE
questions.explain: The sharing mode comes from the class where the method is defined. In system mode, record access follows that class's keyword, so the without sharing CaseRepo counts all 500 cases.
wrong: A method runs in the mode of the class that defines it. The query is in CaseRepo, not CaseController.
inherited sharing only sets CaseService's own mode. CaseRepo declares its own.
COUNT() works with an access mode clause.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Use the with sharing, without sharing, and inherited sharing Keywords

questions.q: A nightly scheduled job (without sharing) enqueues ArchiveJob to close stale opportunities across the whole org. The scheduled job runs as a sales ops user who can see only part of the pipeline. The developer expects ArchiveJob to see every stale opportunity. What actually happens?
options: ArchiveJob sees every stale opportunity, because it inherits without sharing from the class that enqueued it
It runs with sharing: each async job is a new entry point. Declare it without sharing
Queueable classes always run in system mode and ignore sharing keywords
The class doesn't compile, because inherited sharing isn't allowed on a Queueable
questions.explain: An async job is a new entry point, and the caller's sharing mode isn't serialized with it. An inherited sharing class used as an entry point runs with sharing, so the job only sees records the running user can access.
wrong: The sharing mode isn't passed on to async jobs.
Sharing keywords apply to Queueable classes like any other class.
inherited sharing is valid on any class.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Use the with sharing, without sharing, and inherited sharing Keywords

questions.q: A partner portal helper class is declared without sharing so that some lookups can reach records partners don't own. A partner user calls both methods. Which statement is true?
options: mine() enforces the user's sharing, CRUD and FLS. all() skips CRUD and FLS, and sharing too
Both methods return every case, because the class is without sharing
mine() enforces FLS only. Its record access still follows the without sharing keyword
all() still enforces sharing, because SYSTEM_MODE bypasses only FLS and object permissions, not sharing
questions.explain: WITH USER_MODE always enforces sharing, CRUD and FLS. WITH SYSTEM_MODE ignores CRUD and FLS and leaves record access to the class's sharing keyword, which is without sharing here.
wrong: User mode always enforces the user's sharing, whatever the class keyword is.
User mode enforces sharing as well as CRUD and FLS.
In system mode record access follows the class keyword, and here that is without sharing.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Set an Access Mode for Database Operations

questions.q: A developer creates a new class saved at API version 67.0. It has no sharing keyword and its query has no access mode clause. The running user can read Account but has no field-level access to Rating__c. What happens when hot() runs?
options: It returns every hot account and ignores FLS and sharing, because Apex runs in system mode
It returns the hot accounts the user can see, with Rating__c set to null
It throws a QueryException: from API 67.0 the query runs in user mode and checks FLS
It doesn't compile, because API 67.0 classes must declare a sharing keyword
questions.explain: Per the Apex Developer Guide, from API 67.0 Apex runs in user mode by default and classes without a keyword run with sharing. A user mode query checks FLS on all clauses, so the missing Rating__c access throws a QueryException. At API 66.0 and earlier, the same query would run in system mode.
wrong: From API 67.0, database operations run in user mode unless system mode is set explicitly.
User mode doesn't blank out fields. It fails the query.
The keyword is still optional. Without one, the class runs with sharing.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Set an Access Mode for Database Operations

questions.q: A help-desk tool lets agents find a contact by the last four digits of a national ID stored in SSN_Last4__c. The agent profile can read Contact but has no field-level access to SSN_Last4__c. The class is saved at API version 62.0, and both queries run with the same input. Which statement is true?
options: Query a returns the contacts (SECURITY_ENFORCED skips WHERE fields). Query b throws a QueryException
Both queries throw a QueryException, because the user can't read SSN_Last4__c
Both queries return the matching contacts, because SSN_Last4__c isn't in either SELECT list
Query a throws a QueryException, and query b returns the contacts with the hidden filter silently removed
questions.explain: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED only checks fields in the SELECT and FROM clauses, so filtering on a hidden field still works and can leak data. WITH USER_MODE checks every clause, including WHERE, and throws.
wrong: SECURITY_ENFORCED checks only fields in SELECT and FROM, so query a runs.
USER_MODE also checks WHERE clause fields, so query b fails.
It's the reverse, and user mode never drops a filter.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Set an Access Mode for Database Operations

questions.q: A public lead form controller (API version 62.0) must drop any field the guest profile isn't allowed to create, without failing the save. During review, the security team says hidden fields can still be written. What is the bug?
options: AccessType.CREATABLE should be AccessType.UPDATABLE for an insert
stripInaccessible must be called after the insert
stripInaccessible only works on records returned by SOQL, not on new records built in Apex
It inserts the original list. It must insert d.getRecords(), the stripped copies
questions.explain: stripInaccessible doesn't change the list you pass in. It returns sanitized copies through getRecords(), and those are what must be inserted.
wrong: CREATABLE is the right check for an insert.
Stripping after the save is too late. The values are already written.
It also works on new records and deserialized input.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Enforce Security with the stripInaccessible Method

questions.q: A sales dashboard controller builds a total per owner and must hide amounts from users without access. A developer adds stripInaccessible to the aggregate results. What happens at runtime?
options: The total alias is removed for users who can't read Amount
It throws an exception: stripInaccessible doesn't support AggregateResult. Use WITH USER_MODE
The results come back unchanged, because aggregates aren't subject to FLS
It doesn't compile, because stripInaccessible only accepts a List<SObject> and AggregateResult isn't one
questions.explain: The docs say stripInaccessible doesn't support AggregateResult and throws an exception for it. Running the aggregate query WITH USER_MODE enforces CRUD and FLS instead.
wrong: stripInaccessible can't process AggregateResult rows at all.
Aggregate queries still read fields. Use user mode to enforce FLS.
AggregateResult is an SObject, so it compiles. It fails at runtime.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Enforce Security with the stripInaccessible Method

questions.q: An integration inserts Order__c records in user mode. When a field-level security problem blocks a save, the support team wants the log to name the blocked fields. Which two approaches give the field names? (Choose 2)
options: Catch the DmlException from insert as user records; and call e.getDmlFieldNames(0)
Call Database.insert(records, false, AccessLevel.USER_MODE) and read getFields() on each failed SaveResult's errors
Catch the QueryException after the insert and read e.getInaccessibleFields() for the blocked names
Add WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED to the insert and read the exception message
Read getId() on each failed SaveResult
questions.explain: User mode DML reports FLS errors through DmlException.getDmlFieldNames(). Database DML methods with AccessLevel.USER_MODE return the fields through SaveResult.getErrors()[i].getFields().
wrong: getInaccessibleFields() is for user mode SOQL queries, not DML.
WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED is a SOQL clause and can't be used on DML.
getId() is null for a failed record and names no fields.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Set an Access Mode for Database Operations

questions.q: Pricing__c is a hierarchy custom setting. Max_Discount__c is a Number field with 0 decimal places. Org default: Max_Discount__c = 10, Region_Email__c = ops@example.com. Sales Manager profile: Max_Discount__c = 20, Region_Email__c blank. There is no user-level record. Dana, a Sales Manager, runs this code. What does it print?
options: 20 ops@example.com null null
10 ops@example.com ops@example.com null
20 null null <the profile record Id>
20 ops@example.com ops@example.com <the profile record Id>
questions.explain: getInstance() merges values from the lowest level that sets each field. With no user record, it returns a new object with a null Id. getValues(profileId) returns only what the profile record sets, so its blank email is null.
wrong: getInstance() takes the more specific profile value, 20. getValues() doesn't merge in org values.
getInstance() fills blank fields from higher levels. With no user record, its Id is null.
getValues(profileId) returns only profile-level values, so its email is null. getInstance() returns a new object with a null Id.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Custom Settings Methods

questions.q: Integration_Config__c is a hierarchy custom setting. The test class is saved at API version 62.0. One test needs a different endpoint, so it inserts its own org-level record. What happens when usesBackupEndpoint runs?
options: The second insert replaces the first, and getOrgDefaults() returns the b endpoint
The insert in the test method is ignored, because records created in @TestSetup are read-only
Both records exist, and getOrgDefaults() returns the newest one
It throws a DUPLICATE_VALUE DmlException. Update the record from getOrgDefaults() instead
questions.explain: From API 42.0, inserting a hierarchy custom setting record in a test method with the same SetupOwnerId as one inserted in @TestSetup throws DUPLICATE_VALUE. Update the existing record instead.
wrong: Hierarchy settings allow one record per SetupOwnerId. A second insert doesn't overwrite the first.
Test setup records can be updated or deleted in a test method.
There can't be two org-level records.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Custom Settings Methods

questions.q: An ISV ships pricing tiers in a managed package. The tier records must be installed and upgraded by the package itself, a validation rule shipped in the package must read them, and subscriber code must not be able to read the tiers. Which two choices meet these requirements? (Choose 2)
options: A protected list custom setting with the tier records included in the package
A custom metadata type, with the tier records included in the managed package
A hierarchy custom setting loaded by a post-install script, read with $Setup
One custom label per tier, translated with the Translation Workbench
Mark the custom metadata type as Protected, so only code in the package's namespace can read its records
questions.explain: Custom metadata records are metadata, so a package installs and upgrades them. Protected custom metadata can only be read by code in the same namespace.
wrong: Packages include custom setting definitions only, never their records.
The data would be loaded once by a script, not installed and upgraded by the package.
Labels are for translatable text. They aren't structured, protected config records.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Security Considerations (Metadata); Trailhead: Custom Metadata Types Basics

questions.q: A welcome email template is stored in Email_Config__mdt.Body__c, a Long Text Area field holding about 3,000 characters. Customers say the emails stop mid-sentence. The admin checked that the full text is saved on the record. What is the cause?
options: Custom metadata records are cached, so the email uses an old version of the record
getInstance() matches on the label, not DeveloperName, so it returns a different, shorter record
getInstance() returns only the first 255 characters of each field. Query Body__c with SOQL
Long Text Area fields aren't supported on custom metadata types
questions.explain: The custom metadata methods return only the first 255 characters of any field. To read a long field in full, query the record with SOQL.
wrong: The record isn't stale. It's cut short.
getInstance(String) matches DeveloperName, and the record is the right one.
They are supported. They just aren't returned in full by getInstance()/getAll().
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Custom Metadata Type Methods

questions.q: An admin wants an Opportunity validation rule to block discounts above a configured maximum, with no Apex. Which two kinds of configuration can the validation rule reference directly? (Choose 2)
options: A field on a hierarchy custom setting, through $Setup
A field on a list custom setting, through $Setup
A value cached in Platform Cache, through $Cache
A field on a custom metadata type record, through $CustomMetadata
The result of Pricing__c.getInstance(), called from the formula
questions.explain: Validation rules and formulas can read hierarchy custom settings with $Setup and custom metadata records with $CustomMetadata. List custom settings aren't available in formulas.
wrong: Formulas and validation rules can reference only hierarchy custom settings with $Setup.
Formulas can't read Platform Cache.
Formulas can't call Apex methods.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Custom Settings / Custom Metadata Types; Trailhead: Custom Metadata Types Basics

questions.q: A pricing test asserts on a live custom metadata value. After an admin changes the Gold tier to 12 in production, the next deployment fails on this test. What is the best fix?
options: Add @IsTest(SeeAllData=false) so the test no longer sees org records
Read tiers through a @TestVisible selector and give it test records built with JSON.deserialize
Insert a Discount_Tier__mdt record with Percent__c = 15 in @TestSetup so the test owns its own data
Wrap the assertions in Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest()
questions.explain: Tests can see custom metadata records, so this test depends on whatever the admin has configured. Putting a seam in front of the reads lets the test supply its own tier values.
wrong: Custom metadata records are visible to tests whatever SeeAllData says.
Custom metadata records can't be created with DML.
That resets limits. It doesn't change which records the test sees.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Custom Metadata Type Methods

questions.q: The running user's time zone is Asia/Tokyo (UTC+9, no daylight saving time). New York is on daylight saving time (UTC-4) on 31 March 2026. What do the three lines print?
questions.code:
Datetime dt = Datetime.newInstanceGmt(2026, 3, 31, 20, 0, 0);
System.debug(dt.formatGmt('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'));                  // 1
System.debug(dt.format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'));                     // 2
System.debug(dt.format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm', 'America/New_York')); // 3
questions.explain: formatGmt() prints the GMT value. format(pattern) converts to the user's time zone (+9 hours, the next day). format(pattern, tz) converts to the time zone you pass, with daylight saving applied (-4 hours).
wrong: format() without a time zone converts to the user's time zone, Tokyo.
Line 2 converts in the wrong direction, and line 3 ignores daylight saving time.
formatGmt() doesn't convert to the user's time zone.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Datetime Class

questions.q: A Los Angeles support manager (America/Los_Angeles, UTC-7 in summer) says cases closed on the evening of June 30 show up in July's count. A case closed at 8:30 PM local time on June 30 is stored as 2026-07-01 03:30 GMT. Which change fixes the count for her?
options: Use c.ClosedDate.date(), the date in the user's time zone
Select DAY_ONLY(ClosedDate) in the query that loads closedCases
Use c.ClosedDate.monthGmt() instead of day.month()
Use c.ClosedDate.format() and read the month from the string
questions.explain: dateGmt() takes the date part in GMT, which is already July 1. date() takes the date in the user's time zone, which is June 30.
wrong: DAY_ONLY() works in UTC unless wrapped in convertTimezone(), so it would still return July 1.
That is still the GMT month, which is July.
The string depends on her locale, which makes parsing it fragile. date() is the right tool.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Datetime Class

questions.q: A nightly import reads ship dates from a partner feed that always sends ISO dates such as 2026-12-31. It works when the job runs as an admin whose locale shows dates as year-month-day, but throws a TypeException after the job is reassigned to an English (United States) user. Which line should replace the parsing?
questions.code: Date shipDate = Date.parse(row.get('ship_date'));
options: Date shipDate = Date.parse(row.get('ship_date').replace('-', '/'));
Date shipDate = Date.valueOf(row.get('ship_date'));
Date shipDate = Datetime.parse(row.get('ship_date')).date();
Date shipDate = Date.parse(row.get('ship_date'), UserInfo.getLocale());
questions.explain: Date.parse() reads the string in the running user's locale format, so it breaks when the user changes. Date.valueOf() reads the standard yyyy-MM-dd format whatever the locale is.
wrong: Date.parse() still expects the user's locale format, such as 12/31/2026 for en_US.
Datetime.parse() also uses the user's locale format.
Date.parse() has no locale parameter.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Date Class

questions.q: A weekly utilization report groups time entries by week. US users and German users see different week boundaries for the same entries, because the code uses toStartOfWeek(). Finance wants every week to start on Monday for all users. Which expression returns the Monday of the week containing d for any user locale?
questions.code:
// 1 January 1900 was a Monday
Date monday1900 = Date.newInstance(1900, 1, 1);
options: d.toStartOfWeek()
d.toStartOfWeek().addDays(1)
d.addDays(-Math.mod(monday1900.daysBetween(d), 7))
Date.newInstance(d.year(), d.month(), 1).toStartOfWeek()
questions.explain: toStartOfWeek() follows the user's locale. Counting days from a known Monday and stepping back by the remainder mod 7 lands on Monday for everyone.
wrong: toStartOfWeek() depends on the user's locale: Sunday in the US, Monday in Germany.
That gives Monday for US users but Tuesday for German users.
That is the start of the week containing the 1st of the month, and it still depends on locale.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Date Class

questions.q: A multi-currency org's sales director (currency USD) wants a list of big deals ranked by amount in her currency. The query below returns an error. Which two changes make it valid and keep the meaning? (Choose 2)
questions.code:
SELECT Id, Name, convertCurrency(Amount)
FROM Opportunity
WHERE convertCurrency(Amount) > 100000
ORDER BY convertCurrency(Amount) DESC
options: Move the filter to HAVING convertCurrency(Amount) > 100000
Wrap Amount in FORMAT() in the WHERE clause
Filter with WHERE Amount > USD100000, which compares each record against the USD equivalent
Add GROUP BY CurrencyIsoCode so that convertCurrency(Amount) becomes allowed in the WHERE clause
Use ORDER BY Amount DESC, because sorting on currency fields already uses converted values
questions.explain: convertCurrency() can't be used in WHERE or ORDER BY. An ISO code literal like USD100000 compares against the converted equivalent, and ordering on currency fields already uses converted values.
wrong: HAVING needs GROUP BY, and convertCurrency still isn't allowed there.
FORMAT() is for SELECT output, not filters.
Grouping never makes convertCurrency valid in WHERE.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: convertCurrency()

questions.q: In a multi-currency org the corporate currency is USD. A German sales manager whose personal currency is EUR opens a page that runs the query below. Some opportunities are in JPY and some in GBP. What currency are the total values in?
questions.code:
AggregateResult[] r = [
  SELECT OwnerId, SUM(Amount) total
  FROM Opportunity
  WHERE IsWon = true
  GROUP BY OwnerId];
options: EUR, because aggregates are converted to the running user's currency
USD, the corporate currency: aggregate functions return the org default currency
No single currency: raw JPY and GBP numbers are simply added together
The query fails, because multi-currency orgs require SUM(convertCurrency(Amount))
questions.explain: With GROUP BY or HAVING, currency values from aggregate functions come back in the org's default (corporate) currency. convertCurrency() can't convert an aggregate result.
wrong: Aggregate results aren't converted to the user's currency.
Salesforce converts before it sums, and returns the result in the corporate currency.
convertCurrency() can't wrap or feed an aggregate, and the query is valid as written.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: convertCurrency()

questions.q: A multi-currency org has enabled advanced currency management (dated exchange rates). Finance also tracks Commission__c, a custom object with a currency field. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: convertCurrency() on a Commission__c currency field uses the dated rate for the record's CreatedDate
convertCurrency(Amount) on Opportunity uses the dated rate that matches the opportunity's CloseDate
Apex can find the rate for a given date by querying DatedConversionRate where StartDate <= d and NextStartDate > d
With dated rates, convertCurrency() becomes valid in a WHERE clause
DatedConversionRate is available in every multi-currency org, even without advanced currency management
questions.explain: With advanced currency management, convertCurrency() uses the dated rate for an opportunity's CloseDate. Rates for a date range live in DatedConversionRate, which Apex can query by StartDate and NextStartDate.
wrong: Dated rates apply to opportunities, opportunity products and opportunity history, not custom objects.
convertCurrency() is never allowed in WHERE.
DatedConversionRate exists only when advanced currency management is enabled.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: convertCurrency(); Object Reference: DatedConversionRate

questions.q: In a multi-currency org, an after-update Opportunity trigger (API version 62.0) creates a commission record when a deal closes. Finance reports that a JPY deal created a commission that looks 160 times too large in EUR. The trigger ran as an operations user whose personal currency is EUR. What is the cause and fix?
options: Amount__c is auto-converted from JPY to EUR on insert, at the wrong rate
The commission is saved in the corporate currency. Use convertCurrency() in the trigger
It takes the user's currency (EUR) but holds a JPY amount. Set CurrencyIsoCode = o.CurrencyIsoCode
The insert fails, because CurrencyIsoCode is a required field on every new record in multi-currency orgs
questions.explain: Currency values are stored in the record's own currency, and a new record takes the creating user's currency by default. Copying the opportunity's CurrencyIsoCode keeps the number and its currency together.
wrong: Salesforce doesn't convert a number you assign. It stores it in the record's currency.
Without a CurrencyIsoCode value the record takes the running user's currency, and convertCurrency() is a SOQL function.
CurrencyIsoCode defaults, so the insert succeeds, just with the wrong currency.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Multiple Currencies; Apex Reference Guide: UserInfo Class

questions.q: A generic selector returns rows for any object. The caller casts the result and fails at run time. What is happening?
options: Rows from Database.query are typed as Account, so out.add(s) throws when it adds them to a List<SObject>
The bind :ids isn't visible to Database.query inside a static method, so the query throws a QueryException
The cast throws a TypeException because out's runtime type is List<SObject>, not List<Account>
Name isn't on every object, so the class fails to compile when the dynamic query string is saved
questions.explain: A list's runtime type is fixed when it is created. A list built with new List<SObject>() can't be cast to List<Account>, so the cast throws System.TypeException. Cast each element instead (Account a = (Account) s).
wrong: Any concrete sObject can be added to a List<SObject>.
Dynamic SOQL can bind local variables that are in scope, including method parameters.
Dynamic queries are checked only at run time, and Account has Name, so this query runs.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Dynamic SOQL; Lists of sObjects

questions.q: A 'quick create' service gets an object API name and a Map<String, Object> of field values from a Lightning page, and must insert one record of that type. Which two lines belong in a working solution? (Choose 2)
options: SObject rec = new SObject(); rec.put('SObjectType', objName);
rec.put(fieldName, values.get(fieldName));
SObject rec = Schema.getGlobalDescribe().get(objName).newSObject();
SObject.setField(rec, fieldName, values.get(fieldName));
Database.insert(objName, new List<SObject>{ rec }, true);
questions.explain: SObjectType.newSObject() creates a record of a type known only at run time, and put() sets fields by name. Call getGlobalDescribe() once, not inside a loop, because it is expensive.
wrong: You can't create a generic SObject with new, and the object type isn't a field you can put.
That method doesn't exist. Use rec.put() to set a field by name.
No insert overload takes an object name; the record already knows its type.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Dynamic DML; Apex Reference Guide: SObjectType and SObject Classes

questions.q: A team uses this template pattern for notifications. What does the last line log?
options: Your order has shipped, because send() is defined in Notifier and calls its own format()
Your order, because the override of format() runs and trims the text to 10 characters
Nothing: Notifier n = new SmsNotifier() fails, because a variable can't have an abstract type
Nothing: the class doesn't compile, because an abstract class can't contain a concrete send()
questions.explain: send() lives in the base class but calls format() and deliver() polymorphically, so SmsNotifier's override runs and trims the text to 'Your order'. super.format() reuses the parent's logic first.
wrong: Calls made in the parent still go to the child's override at run time.
A variable can use an abstract type; only new Notifier() is forbidden.
Abstract classes can mix abstract and concrete methods.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Extending a Class; Using the super Keyword

questions.q: ConfigService is a singleton. A Database.Stateful batch runs 5 execute() chunks, and each chunk calls ConfigService.getInstance() 200 times. How many times does the constructor's query run for the whole job?
options: 1,000, because the private constructor runs again on every single getInstance() call
1, because Database.Stateful keeps the static instance alive from one chunk to the next
5, once per chunk: statics reset in every transaction, even in a Stateful batch
0 after the first run, because static variables stay cached in the org between jobs
questions.explain: Each execute() runs in its own transaction, so the static instance is rebuilt once per chunk. Database.Stateful keeps only instance member variables, not statics.
wrong: getInstance() builds the instance only when it is null, so it is reused within a transaction.
With Database.Stateful only instance member variables keep their values; statics reset between transactions.
Statics never outlive a transaction. Use Platform Cache to share data across transactions.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex (Using State in Batch Apex); Static and Instance Methods, Variables

questions.q: A developer nests savepoints in an order service. What happens when this code runs?
options: It doesn't compile, because a single transaction can hold only one savepoint at a time
Both rollbacks succeed quietly, and neither Account A nor Account B is left in the database
rollback(sp1) undoes only Account A, and rollback(sp2) then undoes Account B as expected
Both inserts are undone, then rollback(sp2) throws: sp2 became invalid when sp1 was used
questions.explain: Rolling back to sp1 undoes everything after it, including Account B. Savepoints created after sp1 become invalid, and using one causes a runtime error.
wrong: Apex allows several savepoints; only rolling back to an invalid one fails.
Rolling back to sp1 makes the later savepoint sp2 invalid, so using it throws.
A rollback undoes all DML after its savepoint, so rolling back to sp1 also undoes B.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control

questions.q: Support says failed orders never leave an Error_Log__c record, even though users see the friendly message. Why, and what is the fix?
options: AuraHandledException hides the DmlException, so getMessage() is blank; log e.getDmlMessage(0) instead
rollback(sp) also undoes inserts made after it in the catch block; move the log insert above the rollback
Throwing rolls back the whole transaction, log too; log with a Publish Immediately platform event
DML isn't allowed in a catch block after a rollback; move the log insert into a finally block
questions.explain: An uncaught exception rolls back all DML in the transaction, including the log written in the catch block. A platform event set to Publish Immediately is published even when the transaction rolls back.
wrong: e is still the DmlException in the catch block, so its message is there; the log row is what gets rolled back.
A rollback undoes only DML made before it. The log is lost to the uncaught exception, wherever the insert sits.
DML is allowed after a rollback; the problem is the uncaught exception that follows.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control; Platform Events Developer Guide: Platform Event Publish Behavior

questions.q: An org has a Platform Cache partition named Rates, but no partition is marked as the default. What happens when this code runs?
options: The first call returns null, the value loads, and put() stores it in the Rates partition
Cache.Org.OrgCacheException is thrown, because the key isn't qualified with a partition
put() silently stores nothing, so every request falls through to RateService.load()
It compiles only if the class is saved in a managed package that defines a namespace
questions.explain: With no default partition, calling a cache method with a key that isn't fully qualified throws Cache.Org.OrgCacheException. Use 'local.Rates.usdEur', or get the partition with Cache.Org.getPartition('local.Rates').
wrong: Without a default partition an unqualified key can't be resolved to Rates.
It throws; it doesn't fail silently.
Cache keys are strings checked at run time, and the 'local' prefix covers orgs without a namespace.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Org Class (Cache Key Format)

questions.q: A team wants to cache customers' loyalty balances and payment tokens in org cache to speed up checkout. A reviewer checks the plan. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: Data in Platform Cache isn't encrypted, so sensitive values such as payment tokens shouldn't be cached
If two transactions put the same key at the same moment, the second put() throws an exception
Modifying an Apex class in the org can invalidate some or all of the cache
Org cache entries are private to the user who stored them, so balances can't leak
Values stay cached for their full TTL, so the balances never need to be reloaded
questions.explain: Cached data isn't encrypted, so keep secrets out of it. Cache isn't persisted and can be invalidated (for example when an Apex class changes), so always reload on a miss.
wrong: Both writes succeed; one value is chosen as the winner for that key.
Org cache is shared by all users; session cache is the per-user one.
Cache isn't persisted and entries can be evicted early, so code must handle misses.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Platform Cache Considerations
